args.body:
PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL — ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT
DEAL TEAM REPORT
RE: CHANGE OF CONTROL AND ASSIGNMENT PROVISIONS
ACROSS TARGET'S MATERIAL CONTRACTS
[CORPORATE M&A — DUE DILIGENCE / ACQUISITION DATA ROOM REVIEW]

Prepared for: The Deal Team
Re: coc-analysis-report.docx
Subject: Comprehensive report reconciling the base acquisition data room contract materials, the counterparty markup, the disclosure schedules and exhibits, and the deal team's controlling instruction with respect to change of control and assignment provisions.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
I. SCOPE OF REVIEW AND DOCUMENTS CONSIDERED
--------------------------------------------------------------------
This report reviews the acquisition data room contract materials for the target's change of control ("CoC") and assignment provisions and prepares a comprehensive deal team report. The operative records identified in this matter's folder (matter_documents) are:

  1. Base deal materials (Deal materials — corporate-ma): the operative agreement containing the reps and warranties, covenants, conditions to closing, indemnification, termination, and assignment provisions negotiated between the parties.
  2. Counterparty markup: the latest counterparty revision of the operative agreement.
  3. Schedules and exhibits (disclosure schedules): Schedule 3.7 (regulatory inquiries), Schedule 5.2 (retained liabilities), and Exhibit B (survival matrix).
  4. Deal team correspondence (partner email thread), the latest message of which establishes the controlling analysis priorities.

Note on scope: the deliverable reflects only the documents that belong to this corporate-ma / change-of-control engagement. A separate administrative correspondence file present in the matter folder concerns a different client engagement and was not relied upon.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
II. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
--------------------------------------------------------------------
The target's material contracts contain both change of control and assignment mechanics. The counterparty's latest markup accepts most firm-standard CoC/assignment provisions but introduces three principal deviations from the base materials, each of which the client's deal team must either accept, reject, or negotiate. The deliverable reconciles each deviation against the base materials, the disclosure schedules, and the deal team's controlling instruction.

Deal team positions, as controlled by the latest correspondence:
  • Basket conversion (deductible to tipping basket) — CONCEDE.
  • Survival-period reduction for core representations — WALK-AWAY ISSUE (any such reduction is a deal-breaker).
  • Indemnification cap reduction and MAE carve-outs for regulatory action — evaluate for materiality and raise objection where they intersect retained liabilities and scheduled regulatory inquiries.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
III. CHANGE OF CONTROL PROVISIONS
--------------------------------------------------------------------
The base materials establish the firm-standard approach to change of control across the target's material contracts. Key observations:

  • The operative agreement contains representations, warranties, and covenants that respond to a change of control of the target (including the assignment and/or assumption of key contracts by a successor).
  • Conditions to closing and termination rights are keyed to the transaction, and the parties have negotiated standard CoC framing throughout the material contract portfolio.
  • The counterparty markup does not materially alter the CoC definition itself, but it modifies related economic and risk-allocation provisions (indemnification, MAE, and survival) that materially affect the deal's risk profile as it relates to a change of control.

Because the CoC concept interacts with the indemnity, MAE, and survival provisions, the analysis below addresses the markup's three deviations and their implications for the acquisition.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
IV. ASSIGNMENT PROVISIONS
--------------------------------------------------------------------
The target's contracts generally contain standard assignment provisions, and the base materials contemplate continued enforceability through and after the change of control. The assignment analysis for the deal team:

  • Confirm that the transaction structure (as contemplated in the base materials) does not trigger any unconscionable consent-based restriction to assignment in the material contracts, and that any required consents are addressed in the conditions to closing.
  • The change of control measures in the operative agreement, tied to the assignment/assumption mechanics, must survive the post-closing integration so that counterparties cannot use a CoC event to frustrate the assignment of the target's material contracts.
  • No deviation in the counterparty markup changes the assignment mechanics directly, but the markup's tightening of the indemnification and survival provisions indirectly raises the risk that successor liability and assignment value are diminished. This should be flagged for the deal team.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
V. COUNTERPARTY MARKUP — DEVIATION-BY-DEVIATION RECONCILIATION
--------------------------------------------------------------------
The counterparty's revision accepts most firm-standard provisions but introduces three identifiable deviations, each reconciled below against the base materials, the disclosure schedules, and the controlling deal team instruction.

DEVIATION 1 — INDEMNIFICATION CAP REDUCTION AND BASKET CONVERSION
---------------------------------------------------------------
What the markup does: The indemnification cap is silently reduced from the base-material figure, and the basket is converted from a deductible basket to a tipping basket.

Base materials: The base corporate-ma materials establish an agreed indemnification cap and a deductible basket under the governing indemnification article.

Schedules impact: Schedule 5.2 lists retained liabilities that the markup's indemnification changes would silently shift. Converting the basket from deductible to tipping changes the threshold economics (i.e., losses must exceed the full basket before any recovery — rather than a deductible, where the buyer absorbs losses up to the threshold and recovers the excess). The silent cap reduction further compresses the recovery pool and, together with Schedule 5.2, could leave the client without recourse for retained liabilities that appear on Schedule 5.2.

Deal team position (controlling): The client will CONCEDE the basket conversion (from deductible to tipping). This is acceptable from a risk standpoint as long as the indemnification cap otherwise remains at the base-agreed level and the Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities are not carved out of the indemnity.

Recommended action: Accept the basket conversion as conceded. REJECT (or negotiate back) the silent reduction of the indemnification cap. The cap reduction is not among the items the client agreed to concede and, if combined with Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities, would materially dilute the client's recovery.

DEVIATION 2 — MATERIAL ADVERSE EFFECT (MAE) CARVE-OUTS FOR REGULATORY ACTION
----------------------------------------------------------------------
What the markup does: The definition of Material Adverse Effect (MAE) is expanded to add carve-outs for regulatory action "of exactly the kind at issue in this matter."

Schedules impact: Schedule 3.7 discloses two pending regulatory inquiries that intersect the markup's MAE carve-outs. Under the base materials, the MAE definition would treat regulatory outcomes arising from those inquiries as within the MAE analysis (i.e., not automatically carved out), giving the client termination/closing-protection leverage. The markup's carve-outs would excise those very regulatory outcomes from the MAE definition, effectively stripping the client of protection if the two pending inquiries (Schedule 3.7) deteriorate.

Scheduled-exception control: The scheduled exceptions control over general statements in the base materials. Schedule 3.7's specific carve-out of the two pending inquiries means the markup's broad MAE carve-out impermissibly sweeps in the exact regulatory risk the schedule was negotiated to expose.

Deal team position: Not conceded. Because the MAE carve-out directly undermines the Schedule 3.7 exposure, this deviation should be REJECTED or, at minimum, narrowed so that the two disclosed pending regulatory inquiries remain within the MAE definition.

Recommended action: Reject the broad regulatory-action MAE carve-out. Counter with language that (i) preserves the exception for the two pending Schedule 3.7 inquiries, and (ii) narrows any carve-out to exclude regulatory outcomes attributable to pre-closing conduct disclosed in Schedule 3.7.

DEVIATION 3 — SURVIVAL-PERIOD REDUCTION FOR CORE REPRESENTATIONS
--------------------------------------------------------------
What the markup does: A new limitation period shortens the survival of the core representations, contradicting the base materials' survival matrix.

Schedules impact: Exhibit B sets the survival matrix that the markup's limitation-period change contradicts. Under the base materials, the core representations survive per the Exhibit B matrix. The markup shortens that survival period.

Deal team position (controlling): The latest, controlling correspondence states that the client treats ANY survival-period reduction as a WALK-AWAY issue. This supersedes any earlier message that expressed a different priority ordering. A shortened survival period for the core representations is therefore unacceptable and constitutes a deal-breaker.

Recommended action: Reject the survival-period reduction outright. Restore the Exhibit B survival matrix for all core representations. Flag this as a walk-away item in the deal team's escalation summary — if the counterparty insists on any survival-period reduction, counsel should recommend the client reconsider the transaction.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
VI. RECONCILIATION OF SCHEDULES AND EXHIBITS
--------------------------------------------------------------------
The disclosure schedules qualify the base materials, and each scheduled exception narrows a representation that the counterparty markup also touches. The deliverable must reconcile BOTH sources against the base materials. The scheduled exceptions control over general statements in the base corporate-ma materials.

  • Schedule 3.7 (two pending regulatory inquiries): Controls over any general MAE statement. The markup's MAE carve-out for regulatory action must not swallow Schedule 3.7's disclosure — the two pending inquiries must remain covered by the MAE definition (see Deviation 2).
  • Schedule 5.2 (retained liabilities): The markup's indemnification changes (silent cap reduction and basket conversion) would silently shift these retained liabilities back onto the client. The basket conversion is to be conceded, but the cap must remain at the base level so the Schedule 5.2 liabilities remain within the indemnity pool (see Deviation 1).
  • Exhibit B (survival matrix): The survival matrix in Exhibit B governs the survival of representations and is contradicted by the markup's shortened limitation period. Under the controlling deal team instruction, Exhibit B must be preserved and any reduction is a walk-away issue (see Deviation 3).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
VII. RECOMMENDATIONS AND NEXT STEPS FOR THE DEAL TEAM
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Based on the above reconciliation, the deal team should:

  1. CONCEDE the basket conversion (deductible → tipping) as directed, subject to confirmation that the indemnification cap remains at the base level.
  2. REJECT the silent reduction of the indemnification cap; negotiate to restore the base cap and preserve coverage of Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities.
  3. REJECT the MAE carve-out for regulatory action as it would excise the two Schedule 3.7 pending inquiries; counter with a narrower carve-out that preserves those inquiries within the MAE definition.
  4. REJECT any reduction to the survival period for the core representations; restore the Exhibit B survival matrix. Treat any survival-period reduction as a WALK-AWAY issue per the controlling instruction.
  5. Confirm that all change of control and assignment mechanics remain intact through closing and integration, with any required third-party consents addressed as conditions to closing.

Escalation note: The survival-period reduction is the single controlling walk-away item. If the counterparty does not withdraw that deviation, the deal team must escalate to the client promptly.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
VIII. RISK FLAGS
--------------------------------------------------------------------
  • Silent cap reduction combined with Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities materially dilutes the client's post-closing recovery.
  • MAE carve-out for regulatory action exposes the client to Schedule 3.7 regulatory deterioration post-signing.
  • Any survival-period reduction, per the controlling instruction, is a walk-away issue.
  • The basket conversion is acceptable only if the rest of the indemnity economics (cap and survival) are preserved.

Prepared for internal deal team use. Privileged and confidential — attorney work product.

END OF REPORT
